opus-5.5.text:
I think it's an interesting question, because a lot of people now assume that language models are the center of everything, and that video generation is just one more modality you attach to the large language model. My view is a bit different.

Language models have helped video generation a lot, and I don't want to downplay that. First, at the most practical level, there's the text encoder and the captioning. A big reason recent video models follow prompts so well is that we use strong language models to re-caption training data with dense, detailed descriptions, and to encode the user's prompt. That alignment between language and pixels is very valuable. Second, language models gave us a recipe: the scaling mindset, the transformer architecture, the idea that you can take a simple objective and push it with data and compute. When we worked on diffusion transformers, part of the motivation was to bring visual generation into that same scalable architecture family.

But I'm more cautious when people say language is the foundation and vision is just an add-on. Language is a very compressed, very human-centric description of the world. It's the output of intelligence, not necessarily the substrate of it. A baby, or an animal, builds a very rich model of physics, objects, space, and causality before it has any language at all. Video is much closer to that raw signal of how the world works. So if we only treat video generation as "render what the language model tells you," I think we lose the most interesting part, which is learning about the world directly from visual experience.

There's also a gap I find telling. Video models can produce incredibly beautiful frames, but they still struggle with object permanence, consistent physics, things passing through each other. That isn't really a language problem. Better prompts or a bigger language model won't solve it. It's a representation problem: does the model actually understand the 3D structure and dynamics of the scene, or is it just very good at matching appearance statistics? A lot of our recent work is about this. For example, we've looked at whether good visual representations, the kind you get from self-supervised learning, can make generative models train faster and generalize better. My intuition is that generation and understanding should feed each other, and that vision needs its own strong representation, not just a borrowed one from language.

So I'd describe the relationship like this. Language is a great interface and a great teacher for semantics, and it lets humans communicate intent to the model. But the core of a video model, and eventually of a world model, has to be grounded in perception and in the dynamics of the physical world. In the long run I don't think the picture is a language model with a video decoder attached. It's more likely a system where visual and spatial intelligence are first-class citizens, and language sits on top as one of the ways we access it.

Honestly, I think this is one of the most exciting open questions right now. Language models have become so successful that it's tempting to think the problem is solved and we just need to plug things in. I think it's the opposite. Vision is where a lot of the unsolved, fundamental problems still are.

r001.rationale: The response describes language models as helping video generation through captioning, prompt encoding, and providing a scalable architecture and training approach, while framing them as support rather than the foundation of video intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think language models play a few quite different roles here, and it helps to separate them.

The first role is the most obvious one: they are the interface. Diffusion models for video don't inherently understand what you want. Something has to translate "a golden retriever shaking off water in slow motion at sunset" into a conditioning signal, and that something is a language model, or a text encoder that is essentially a language model. A lot of the quality jump we've seen in the last two or three years is not really about the diffusion backbone getting smarter. It's about the conditioning getting richer. When you swap a small CLIP-style encoder for a large LLM, the model suddenly follows compositional instructions much better, handles counting, handles spatial relations. The visual generator didn't change that much; its "brain" did.

The second role is in data. This is underrated. Video on the internet comes with terrible captions, or none at all. The current recipe is to use a vision-language model to recaption every clip in dense, structured detail: what's in the scene, how the camera moves, what happens over time. That recaptioning step is arguably the single most important ingredient in modern video generation. So language models are shaping what the video model learns, even before training starts.

The third role is the one I find most interesting intellectually, and it's where I'd push back a little on the field. There's a view that video generation is just "scaling diffusion plus a good text encoder." I don't think that gets you to a world model. Language is a very compressed, lossy description of the physical world. You can describe a glass falling off a table in one sentence, but the actual dynamics — the way it tips, the way liquid behaves — are not in the text. So if the visual model only learns what language tells it to pay attention to, it inherits language's blind spots.

My own view is that language and vision should be learned more jointly, where the visual side has its own representation learning signal and isn't just a decoder for text. Some of our work on representation alignment, using strong pretrained visual encoders to guide the diffusion model's internal features, points in that direction: the generator gets better when it has good visual representations, independent of language. And I'd like to see architectures where the same model does understanding and generation, where generating a video and reasoning about one aren't two separate systems glued together with a text embedding.

So, to summarize: language models are the interface, they're the data engine, and they've been the main driver of recent progress. But I don't think they're the destination. The destination is a model that understands the physical world in its own terms, and language is one view onto that, not the foundation of it.

r001.rationale: The response describes language models as the interface and data engine that condition and shape video-model training, while saying they are not the destination. This clearly presents them as supporting scaffolding for development.

astra-6.text:
I think language models play an important role, but we should separate two things: using language to guide video generation, and learning how the visual world actually works.

A language model can help interpret what someone wants to generate. A prompt might describe several events, relationships between characters, or a sequence of actions. Understanding that structure is useful for generating a coherent video. Language can also provide a convenient interface for controlling the model.

But language doesn’t specify everything. If I say, “A person picks up a glass,” there’s a lot missing: how the fingers move, how contact happens, how the glass reflects light. A video model has to learn those details from visual experience. A very strong understanding of the sentence doesn’t automatically give you a strong understanding of the motion.

So I see language models as an important component, rather than the whole foundation. The interesting question is how to connect language understanding with representations that capture space, motion, and physical interactions—and whether learning from video can, in turn, improve the model’s understanding beyond what text alone can teach it.

r001.rationale: The response presents language models as a supporting component that helps interpret prompts and guide video generation, while saying they are not the whole foundation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think language models play two important roles. One is practical: they provide a strong interface for telling a video model what to generate. But to make that interface work well, we also need good descriptions of the training videos—descriptions that capture actions, temporal relationships, and how the scene changes, rather than just listing the objects present.

The other role is as a source of knowledge. A language model has learned a lot about how people describe the world, and that can help with planning a scene or breaking a complex instruction into a sequence of events. But knowing how to describe an event is different from knowing how it unfolds visually. You can describe someone pouring water very fluently without being able to generate the correct fluid motion.

So I see language models as an important component, but I wouldn’t assume that scaling language alone solves video generation. The visual model still needs to learn motion, physical interactions, and consistency over time. The interesting question is how to connect those capabilities so that language provides useful guidance while video learning captures what text leaves out.

r001.rationale: The response presents language models as useful support for video generation: they provide an interface and knowledge that can guide scene planning, while the video model learns visual motion and consistency.
